# Yardhand

> A self-hosted gateway: one endpoint for every tool behind it, from MCP servers and REST APIs its owner connected.
> Find a tool by what you want to do, read its input schema, run it. Over MCP at `/mcp`, or over REST here.
> Send `Authorization: Bearer <key>` on every call (one key per client), or an OAuth token the owner approves.

## Start

- MCP clients: connect to `/mcp`. You get `search_tools`, `describe_tool`, `call_tool`, `get_result`,
  `list_upstreams`, `read_resource`, `get_playbook`, and any tools pinned for your key. The server instructions list
  the upstreams you may use, and mark those with a manual. Playbooks are also listed as prompts (slash commands).
- REST clients: `GET /api` links to everything. The usual path is three calls:
  1. `GET /api/tools?q=<what you want to do>`: tools across every upstream, best match first.
  2. `GET /api/tools/{name}`: the tool's description and JSON Schema input.
  3. `POST /api/calls` with `{"tool": "<name>", "arguments": {…}}`, or `POST /api/tools/{name}/calls` with the
     arguments as the whole body. The answer carries the tool's own result (`result.content`, and
     `result.structuredContent` when it declares an output schema).
- Typed clients: `GET /api/tools/openapi.json` describes every tool your key may use as an OpenAPI 3.1 operation.
- The owner manages the gateway in the browser at `/app` (connections, keys, reviews, the call log). Everything there
  is an `/api` route too, but those routes answer only the owner's key: a client key gets 403.

## Manuals, playbooks and links

Some upstreams say more than their tools do:

- A **manual**: how the upstream wants its tools used. Read it once before its tools: `read_resource`
  `gateway://u/<upstream>/manual` (MCP), or `GET /api/manuals/{name}`. `GET /api/manuals` lists them; MCP clients with
  the Skills extension also get them as skills (`skill://<manual>/SKILL.md`). The gateway adds a short note at the
  top saying how its tools and links are named here; the rest is as the upstream wrote it.
- **Playbooks**: the upstream's step-by-step way to do one task (its MCP prompts). `search_tools` (and
  `GET /api/tools?q=…`, in `playbooks`) suggests one when it fits; `get_playbook` or
  `GET /api/playbooks/{name}/messages?arguments={…}` fills it in. Named `<upstream>-<prompt>`.
- **Links** a tool returns, like `cookbook://recipes/123`: read them as they came with `read_resource` or
  `GET /api/resources?uri=…`; the gateway finds the upstream by the scheme. `GET /api/links` lists the kinds.

Reading any of these uses the upstream's credential and is logged like a call, but needs no write scope.

## Pack keys

A key can be locked to a **pack**: a kit for one kind of work, curated by the owner. `GET /api/me` says so (`pack`,
and `packs` when the key opens several). A pack is a small server of its own at one address, `/p/<pack>/`:

- MCP at `/p/<pack>/mcp`, and REST under `/p/<pack>/api`: every `/api` route a key may use (health and sign-in stay
  at the root), with links that stay under that address.
- Its own guide at `/p/<pack>/llms.txt` and OpenAPI document at `/p/<pack>/openapi.json`, rendered at
  `/p/<pack>/docs`. They describe the pack and nothing else: with a pack key, read them rather than this guide.
- The older ways still work: MCP at `/mcp/p/<pack>`, and REST or `/mcp` naming the pack with the `x-gateway-pack`
  header. Plain `/mcp` and `/api` serve the key's default pack.
- A pack's address can change when its owner renames it: the old one keeps answering, and `GET /api/me` gives the
  address it has now (`packs[].mcpUrl`).

A pack key sees only the pack. Over MCP the server is named after the pack and its description opens the server
instructions. It has the gateway's shape: `search_tools`, `describe_tool`, `call_tool` and the others work over the
pack only, and every tool of the pack is listed directly, in the pack's own wording. A key the owner gave
pins of its own lists only those and finds the rest with `search_tools` (`PATCH /api/clients/{id}` with `pins`, by
the pack's names; `pins: null` lists the whole pack again). The pins set for every client never apply inside a pack.

A pack sets some inputs of its tools. An input the pack fills itself is not in the tool's schema: leave it out, a
call that sends it is refused (400). An input the pack gives a default shows that default in the tool's schema; send
your own value to replace it.

A pack can have a skill and playbooks written for it, by its owner, over its own tools:

- Its **skill**, "Working with <title>": what the pack is for, which tool does which job, what is already set, and
  what it can't do. Read it once, before the pack's tools: `read_resource` `skill://<pack>/SKILL.md` (MCP), or
  `GET /api/resources?uri=skill://<pack>/SKILL.md`. `GET /api/me` gives the address (`pack.skill`, null when the
  pack has none), the server instructions name it, and MCP clients with the Skills extension get it as a skill. It
  also opens the pack's guide, `/p/<pack>/llms.txt`.
- Its **own playbooks**: listed first in `GET /api/playbooks` and as prompts, with `upstream: null` and `pack` set,
  under the name the pack gave them (`say-hello`, not `<upstream>-<prompt>`). `search_tools` suggests them, and
  `get_playbook` or `GET /api/playbooks/{name}/messages?arguments={…}` fills one in with your arguments and the
  pack's own values. They belong to no connection: `?upstream=<id>` leaves them out, and no connection counts them.

Playbooks, manuals and calls stay inside the pack too. A call to anything else is refused (403) and logged; the
per-upstream passthrough (`/u/{id}/mcp`) is refused too. A pack key opens only the links its tools returned in the
last day (through `/u/{upstream}/r/…` and `read_resource`), so `GET /api/links` is empty for it. Its connections
(`GET /api/upstreams`, `list_upstreams`) count only what the pack holds: its tools under the pack's names, its
playbooks and its manuals. A search that matches nothing in the pack says what the pack covers: `hint` on
`GET /api/tools?q=…`, and over MCP `Nothing in <pack> matches "<query>". This pack covers: …`. Ask again by one of
those, or say it can't be done with this pack. Access can end: a 403 then says which pack, the day it ended and to
ask the owner for a new invite; over MCP the connection still opens and says the same. Once the owner has extended
it, send a request that was refused with a new `Idempotency-Key`: the old one answers the refusal again for a day.

A key that opens several packs has one connection per pack, and is refused (403) a pack it doesn't open with the
addresses of those it does. An `Idempotency-Key` is remembered per key and route, not per pack: sent again with the
same body at another of the key's packs, it answers the first result again. So use a new `Idempotency-Key` for each
new request.

The owner's key at a pack's address (or with the header) is answered as a write key of that pack: what its agents
see. Routes that manage the gateway answer 403 there. From the root, `GET /api/tools?pack=<pack>` searches as the
pack's keys do, and with `as=<client id>` as that one key.

## Writing a pack

With the owner's key, at the root (a pack's own address answers 403 to these), an agent can write a pack as the owner
does in `/app`. Every save is checked first and refused whole when what it sends is wrong: a 400 whose `detail`
starts `Not saved:`, with one entry per problem under `errors`. Nothing is half saved.

- **Variables**: named values of the pack. `PUT /api/packs/{name}/variables` with
  `{"variables": [{"name": "city", "value": "Lisbon"}]}` replaces the whole set. A name is lowercase letters, digits
  and `_`; a value is text, a number or true/false.
- **Inputs**: `PATCH /api/packs/{name}/tools/{tool}` with `fixed` (the pack fills the input on every call, and its
  keys never see it), `defaults` (shown with the pack's value, which the agent may replace) and `person` (hidden, and
  filled with one variable, written `{{open}}city}}` and nothing else, as it is for whoever calls). An input in none
  is the agent's. A value writes a variable as `{{open}}city}}`; a value that is one variable and nothing else keeps
  the variable's type. `{tool}` is the name the pack calls the tool: its alias, else `<upstream>.<tool>`.
- **Per person**: an input in `person` takes the person's own value, else the pack's, else nothing is sent and the
  tool's own default applies. A variable only such inputs read may have `"value": null`. Set a person's values when
  sharing (`values` on `POST /api/packs/{name}/people`) or later with `PUT /api/packs/{name}/people/{client}/values`;
  each is checked against every input that reads it. A person's value is theirs to know, so an input that limits
  what they reach (an account) belongs in `fixed`.
- **A playbook**: `POST /api/packs/{name}/playbooks` with `{"name": "find-roles", "markdown": "…"}`;
  `PUT` and `DELETE /api/packs/{name}/playbooks/{playbook}` replace and remove one. The Markdown opens with front
  matter (`title`, `description`, `arguments`), then the steps:

  ```markdown
  ---
  title: Find roles
  description: Finds open roles in a city and lists the best five.
  arguments:
    - name: role
      description: The kind of role, e.g. product designer.
      required: true
  ---

  1. Run `jobs.search_postings` with `query` set to {{open}}role}}, in {{open}}city}}.
  2. List the five best matches, newest first.
  ```

  The text writes an argument or one of the pack's variables as `{{open}}name}}` and numbers its steps. It names the
  pack's tools in backticks, by the names the pack calls them: only a name in backticks is read as a tool.
- **The skill**: `PUT /api/packs/{name}/skill` with `{"markdown": "…"}`. A pack has one, "Working with <title>", in
  six `##` sections: What it is for, Which tool for which job, Values already set, Playbooks, Gotchas, What it can't
  do. Send the sections only: the gateway writes the front matter and the heading from the pack.
- **Try a draft**: `POST /api/packs/{name}/checks` with `{"kind": "playbook", "markdown": "…"}` (or
  `"kind": "skill"`) answers `findings` and saves nothing.

What the checks say:

- Refused, as an `error`: a tool in backticks that is not in the pack, or written by its own name where the pack
  gives it another; a `{{open}}word}}` in a playbook or the skill that is neither an argument nor a variable; front
  matter that can't be read; a fixed or default value the tool's input schema does not take.
- Saved, with a `warning` in `findings`: a tool a read-only key can't run, a name shaped like a tool that is none,
  a playbook past 12 steps, a section the skill leaves out.
- In a fixed or default value, a `{{open}}word}}` the pack has no variable for is sent as written, with a warning:
  a tool whose own input is a template keeps working. In a playbook or the skill nothing is sent as written, so
  there it is an error. That holds inside fenced code blocks too: there is no escape to keep a `{{open}}word}}` as
  written.

`GET /api/packs/{name}` shows the pack as it stands: `findings`, `ownPlaybooks`, `skill`, and `flags` once a tool
changed under a text. A text is never blocked by a tool that moves: it is flagged, and saving it again clears the
flag. The pack's keys get what you wrote at once (see Pack keys).

## Rules worth knowing

- Tool names are `<upstream>.<tool>`, e.g. `cookbook.research_recipes`.
- Search returns only tools that clearly match what you asked. A question that matches nothing answers `count: 0`
  (`No tools match.` over MCP): ask again in other words, and if it stays empty there is no tool for it here. A
  gateway with fewer than 50 tools, or without search by meaning, has no such bar: it answers with its nearest tools
  and every keyword hit, however weak.
- A tool that changes things (`needsWrite: true`, `[changes things]` in MCP) needs a key with write scope; a
  read-only key never sees those tools.
- The owner can switch tools off: one tool, a group of a connection's tools, or everything on a connection that
  changes or deletes things. An off tool is left out of lists and searches; calling it anyway is a 403 whose `detail`
  says which switch is off. Ask the owner rather than looking for another way round.
- Over MCP, a result bigger than your key's cap is cut: you get page 1 and a call id; `get_result` (or
  `GET /api/calls/{id}/result?page=2`) gives the rest for an hour. REST answers are never cut.
- `POST` runs accept `Idempotency-Key`: a retried request with the same key answers the first result again. A new
  request needs a new key: the same one with another body is a 422.
- Calls are rate-limited per key (`RateLimit` headers; 429 with `Retry-After` when over).
- Errors are `application/problem+json` with a `detail` that says what to do next: arguments that don't match
  the tool's input schema are a 400 listing each bad field in `errors`, before the upstream is called. A tool
  that ran and reported its own failure answers 200 with `status: "tool_error"` and `result.isError: true`.
- Links in a result that point at an upstream's own host are rewritten to `/u/{upstream}/r/<path>`: open them
  with the same key (read-only, through the gateway).
- A connection's tools come in groups (`groups` on `GET /api/upstreams`, printed by `list_upstreams`): narrow a
  search to one with `group` and `upstream` (`search_tools`, or `GET /api/tools?upstream=…&group=…`).
- In lists a tool has a short `summary`; `GET /api/tools/{name}` gives the full `description` and schemas.
- Lists are HAL: follow `_links.next` until it is absent.
- Send W3C trace context (a `traceparent` header on REST, `_meta.traceparent` on MCP) and each call is recorded as a
  span inside your own trace; without it, each call is a trace of its own. Only metadata is traced, never arguments
  or results.
